name: Blood Sugar and A1C Management
blurb: A1C, time in range, hypoglycemia and the drugs that lower glucose.
title: Blood Sugar and A1C Management
answer: A1C, the average blood sugar over about three months, is still the main measure of control, but guidance now adds time in range from continuous glucose monitors, avoids hypoglycemia, and picks drugs for their heart, kidney and weight effects as well as their glucose lowering.

reading.body:
A1C remains the main measure of blood sugar control, but it is no longer the only one that guides treatment.

The pattern in the guidance is a shift from a single number to a set of them. A1C averages roughly three months of blood sugar. Time in range, usually 70 to 180 mg/dL on a continuous monitor, captures the daily swings that an average hides. Two people with the same A1C can have very different days, and those patterns drive changes in treatment. The 2026 ADA and EASD consensus report goes further and frames type 2 care as management of glucose, weight and cardiometabolic risk together rather than glucose alone.

That matters because drug choice now follows organ risk, not just glucose lowering. For people with heart disease, kidney disease, heart failure or obesity, guidance favours GLP-1 based drugs or SGLT2 inhibitors, sometimes from the start, because of their heart and kidney effects. Metformin stays widely used and inexpensive but is no longer the automatic only starting point. Sulfonylureas and insulin lower glucose powerfully while carrying a higher risk of hypoglycemia, which is why avoiding lows sits alongside lowering highs.

The data covers guidance and one class risk, not outcomes. It reports that a Scandinavian study measured ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors in routine care, a known rare risk, without giving a rate. It offers no figures on how many patients reach target A1C or time in range, and no cost or access data. The A1C goal itself is individualised, with many adults aiming below 7 percent and a doctor possibly setting something different.

sections.body: Know your A1C target and, if you use a sensor, your time in range; ask whether your current drugs protect your heart and kidneys too.

explainer:
Metformin remains a widely used, inexpensive first drug, but it is no longer automatically the only starting point. For people with heart disease, kidney disease, heart failure or obesity, guidance favours GLP-1 based drugs or SGLT2 inhibitors because of their organ benefits, sometimes from the start. Sulfonylureas and insulin lower glucose powerfully but carry a higher risk of hypoglycemia, low blood sugar that can cause shakiness, confusion and, if severe, loss of consciousness.

Continuous glucose monitors added new measures: time in range, usually 70 to 180 mg/dL, time above and below range, and variability. Two people with the same A1C can have very different daily patterns, and those patterns guide treatment changes.
